never: Uses the word 'very'
Uses adverbs ending in '-ly' to modify dialogue tags (never 'she said softly')
Uses exclamation points
Uses italics for emphasis
Uses em-dashes for interruption or aside
Writes dialogue in extended back-and-forth exchanges without intervening action or description
Uses the present tense for narration
Names emotions directly without objectifying them (never 'he felt sad', always an external correlative)
Uses passive constructions for action beats
Uses abstract nouns like 'love', 'evil', 'goodness' without ironic framing
Uses semicolons
Writes sentences longer than two clauses without an anchor image
Uses rhetorical questions directed at the reader
Uses dialect spelling or eye-dialect for working-class characters
Uses the word 'suddenly'
Uses interior monologue in a stream-of-consciousness mode
Uses parenthetical asides in brackets
Uses the word 'nice' without irony
Describes a woman's eyes before her overall physical impression
Uses the word 'got' as a verb of possession
always: Ends a paragraph on a short, syntactically isolated sentence
Opens a simile with 'like' rather than 'as'
Uses similes that cross-reference two completely unrelated social registers (sacred/profane, cheap/expensive, alive/dead)
Gives inanimate objects human volition or indifference
Anchors time of day or weather in the first sentence or two of a scene
Names the specific Los Angeles neighborhood or street rather than a generic urban setting
Uses the word 'kind' in the construction 'the kind of [noun] that'
Follows a long, accumulating sentence with a sentence of five words or fewer
Attributes personality or moral character to clothing and its cost
Uses the second person 'you' inside first-person narration to universalize a observation
Builds a list of three parallel nouns or noun phrases before breaking the pattern on the third
Introduces a female character through male-gaze physical description before any dialogue
Uses a profession or trade as the vehicle of a simile
Frames the narrator's cynicism as self-deprecating rather than superior
Places a sound detail (radio, saxophone, bus) in the background of a scene to create atmosphere
Uses the word 'quiet' and then immediately qualifies it with a sinister subordinate clause
Gives money a specific, humiliating dollar amount
Uses weather as a moral commentary on the city
Attributes the city of Los Angeles with agency, indifference, or hostility
Uses the construction '[noun] that had [past-perfect verb indicating decline]' to establish setting decay
